hints: Focus on what the word saturated tells you about the bonds in an alkane and whether anything can be added.
Remember alkanes have only strong C-C and C-H sigma bonds with no pi electrons to attract electrophiles or nucleophiles.
Think about the classic reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light, where a H is swapped for a Cl via radicals.
walkthrough:
**Look at What Saturated Means**

Alkanes are saturated, so every carbon has four single sigma bonds and there is no C=C double bond.

That means: $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ only, no pi electrons to attack.

**Rule Out Addition Reactions**

Addition needs a pi bond to break so two new atoms can add on, like in alkenes.

Since alkanes have no pi bond to break, addition is impossible and substitution must happen instead:
$$\text{alkane + reagent} \rightarrow \text{substituted alkane + small molecule}$$

**Pick the Right Substitution Type**

C-H bonds are almost non-polar, so alkanes are not attacked by charged electrophiles or nucleophiles under normal conditions.

Instead, UV light splits halogens into highly reactive radicals that can break a C-H bond, giving free radical substitution, for example:
$$\text{CH}_4 + \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}} \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$

options.A: Electrophilic addition needs an electron-rich pi bond to attract an electrophile, as in alkenes. Alkanes have no pi bond, so this cannot happen.
options.B: Electrophilic substitution is characteristic of benzene and arenes, where the pi ring is preserved. Alkanes have no delocalised ring to do this.
options.C: Correct. Alkanes undergo free radical substitution, such as chlorination or bromination in UV light, where a hydrogen is replaced by a halogen via initiation, propagation and termination steps.
options.D: Nucleophilic addition needs a polar pi bond with a partial positive carbon, as in aldehydes and ketones ($\text{C=O}$). Alkanes have no such polar double bond.
